title: Biomedical Publishing Metrics as a Barrier to Knowledge Dissemination
content: Abstract:  The Journal Impact Factor (JIF) is an outdated biomedical metric that hinders knowledge dissemination. Relying on citation counts creates a skewed, easily manipulated system with a temporal lag that ignores global equity. Frontline clinicians consume research to improve care but rarely generate citations, meaning the JIF cannot capture real-world clinical utility. To ensure rankings reflect true value, publishers must adopt a multi-dimensional matrix prioritizing usage-based Altmetrics, such as verified downloads and views, to instantly measure global clinical application.

title: Unlocking knowledge: diamond open access publishing - UNESCO Digital Library
content: Diamond Open Access (OA) is an equitable scholarly publishing model that treats knowledge as a digital public good, with no fees for readers or authors. Built on shared infrastructure, open licensing, and community governance, it supports non-profit, academically driven publishing while allowing commercial providers to deliver specific services. Like Open Educational Resources (OER), Diamond OA promotes equitable access, collaboration, and multilingual knowledge sharing. It can strengthen national and institutional Open Access strategies while connecting OER, Open Data, and open research software into interoperable knowledge ecosystems. This brief examines Diamond OA infrastructure and provides practical policy guidance for Member States and institutions.

title: From access to impact: the gold OA advantage | Springer Nature
content:
"This white paper explores the effect of different routes to OA on the reach and impact of articles in hybrid journals. The data shows that, 8 years on from our first major study into this topic, there is still a substantial advantage for gold OA articles across all disciplines (measured by downloads, citations and Altmetric Attention Score) over both non-OA articles and green OA articles. 4

The analysis of 204,781 articles published in 1,812 hybrid Springer Nature journals in 2023 also shows how gold OA can accelerate the number of downloads over time and the diversity of geographic readership, leading to faster impact and greater equity in access."

title: Gold OA reaches record 44pc share of global research output - Research Information
content:
"Gold open access (OA) articles reached their highest-ever share of global research output in 2025, accounting for 44% of all journal articles, reviews and conference papers published worldwide.

Nearly two million research articles were published through gold OA during the year, making it the principal driver of immediate, freely available access to research, according to the latest release of the STM Open Access Dashboard.

The Dashboard, which tracks the uptake of different routes to OA between 2015 and 2025, shows that gold OA has quadrupled over the past decade."

title: Open Access Library and Information Science (LIS) Journals Indexed in the Directory of Open Access Journals (DOAJ): An Analytical Study | Annals of Library and Information Studies
content: Abstract: The study examines the trends and current status of Open Access (OA) research journals listed in the Directory of Open Access Journals (DOAJ) in the field of Library and Information Science (LIS) from 2003 to mid-2026. It investigates the profile of OA LIS journals, publishing trends, publishing practices, open access policies, licensing practices and journal scope through thematic analysis of keywords. The study identified 231 OA LIS journals published in 32 languages by 200 publishers across 55 countries globally. The study adopted a descriptive research approach and data were collected from the DOAJ and verified through the official journal websites where required. The collected data were compiled, organised, tabulated and analysed using Microsoft Excel. The findings provide insights into the growth of LIS journals, geographical distribution, publishers, language profile, publication mode, peer-review practices, article processing charges (APCs), copyright ownership, Creative Commons licensing, self-archiving policies, digital preservation mechanisms, Digital Object Identifier (DOI) availability and other publishing infrastructure adopted by OA LIS journals.

content: Abstract: Thi study examined Perceived Ease of Access (PEOA) and Use of Open Access Resources (OAR) by Library and Information Science (LIS) postgraduate students in universities in Southwest, Nigeria. The study adopted a quantitative research method and correlational research design to answer two research questions and one hypothesis. The population consisted of 227 postgraduate students from five universities: Adeleke University (AU) - 22, Babcock University (BU)-35, Lead City University (LCU)-30, Tai Solarin University (TASUED)-30 and University of Ibadan (UI)-110. Data were collected using a structured questionnaire administered through the total enumeration technique. The collected data were analysed using both descriptive and inferential statistical methods. The findings revealed that the largest respondents were: UI (49%), females (50.7%), age group 26-30 (39.4%), and single (55.9%). title: Strengthening Trust and Leadership: Reflections on National Institutes of Health (NIH) 2026 Community Days: Securing NIH Controlled-Access Data and Our Data Protection Journey | Data Science at NIH
content: "On April 13 and 14, I had the privilege of leading the National Institutes of Health (NIH) 2026 Community Days: Securing NIH Controlled-Access Data webinars to engage directly with our stakeholders, researchers, and the broader public about the critical work we’re undertaking to protect controlled-access data. These sessions were designed to foster transparency around our security and operational standards, update the community on new resources and requirements, and reinforce our shared responsibility in safeguarding participant trust. I am deeply grateful for the vibrant participation and thoughtful questions that were raised, which underscores the importance and urgency of our mission. Protecting participants’ trust requires one standard: secure, consistent protections for NIH controlled-access data—whether it is processed within a NIH Controlled-Access Data Repository (CADR) or a research institution’s IT systems. This principle drove the Extramural Community Days agenda, where we discussed not only what needs to be done, but why rigorous data protection is more essential than ever. content: Abstract: Introduction: Scholarly communities are experiencing increased emphasis on research data sharing and reuse. Given the range of available data repositories and variability in the use of persistent identifiers (PIDs) for individuals and institutions, aggregating datasets by researchers at a specific institution is a significant challenge. We developed a reproducible workflow to evaluate 1) data repository use by researchers at our institutions, 2) metrics of reuse, and 3) quality of metadata records. Methods: We used the DataCite REST API to locate metadata records for datasets with creator affiliation names that matched our institutions. We performed substantial cleaning and deduplication before comparing repository use, citations, usage metrics, and metadata completeness. Results: The most common data repositories were Dryad, Harvard Dataverse, figshare, Zenodo, ICPSR, and one institution’s institutional repository. View, download, and citation counts were available from a limited number of repositories, with some discrepancies between different citation reporting methods. title: Recommendations for Revising the Open Access Classification System in OpenAlex | Zenodo
content: "The open access (OA) color classification system used by Unpaywall (i.e., Gold, Green, Hybrid, Bronze, and closed) was introduced in 2018 and has since become widely used across the ecosystem, including by Scopus, Web of Science, Dimensions, and numerous funders and institutions worldwide. However, the scholarly communication landscape has changed significantly since these categories were defined and the limits of this system are proving problematic. In particular, the current system struggles with research outputs that are not journal publications, relies too heavily on journal-level policies rather than work-level attributes, conflates business models with access status, and is difficult to accurately operationalize in an environment where journals regularly change the OA status of publications en masse. The OpenAlex Colors Working Group was convened by the OpenAlex Community Advisory Board in January 2026 to evaluate these limitations and recommend a revised framework. title: Wiley research publishing revenue jumps 12pc on OA growth and Emerald acquisition - Research Information
content:
"Wiley has reported 4% growth in its research division for the first quarter of its 2027 financial year, with publishing revenue climbing 12% as strong demand for open access and the addition of Emerald Publishing boosted the business.

Research revenue reached $293 million for the three months ended 31 July 2026, up 4% both on a reported basis and at constant currency.

Research Publishing revenue increased 12% at constant currency, driven by what Wiley described as strong growth in gold open access and AI licensing, alongside a $13 million contribution from Emerald Publishing following completion of the acquisition during the quarter.

The performance helped offset a 30% decline in Research Solutions revenue, which faced a tough comparison with the same period last year because of AI licensing income. Research Solutions generated $4 million in AI licensing revenue during the quarter, compared with $16 million a year earlier."

title: Six UK universities renew unlimited open access deal with JMIR Publications - Research Information
content:
"Six UK universities have renewed an unlimited open access publishing agreement with JMIR Publications through Jisc, extending the arrangement until July 2027.

Newcastle University, the University of Leeds, University of Manchester, University of Nottingham, University of Southampton and University of Warwick have renewed their participation in JMIR Publications’ Flat-Fee Unlimited Open Access Publishing Agreement.

The model replaces individual article processing charges (APCs) with an institutional publishing subscription, allowing eligible researchers at participating universities to publish without paying an APC.

Corresponding authors affiliated with the six institutions can publish across JMIR Publications’ portfolio of more than 30 Gold Open Access journals, covering research across the digital health sector. The renewed agreement runs until 31 July 2027.

JMIR said the subscription model is designed to reduce the administrative and financial barriers associated with individual APC payments, while giving institutions greater predictability over their open access publishing costs."

title: Project MUSE - The Data Rescue Project: A Crowdsourced Effort to Preserve At-Risk US Federal Data
content: Abstract: The US federal government is the world's largest data publisher. Since Trump's second inauguration, these data are threatened because their scope contravenes regime ideology and the offices that maintain these datasets no longer have adequate staff to preserve and provide access to the data. The Data Rescue Project was launched in 2025 as a community response to this crisis. We organized volunteers to work on data rescues, focusing especially on social data to fill an identified gap in other rescue efforts and emphasizing curation of the datasets for long-term data preservation. Through community-building, we became a coordinating body for the data rescue movement, streamlining communication and preventing duplication of effort in the US and internationally. In this article, we use the Data Rescue Project as a case study on building coalitions to push back against the destruction of digital information. Moreover, the US is not unique in its need for these efforts. The need to rapidly capture data from natural disasters, war zones, or unforeseen crises is a component of the digital preservation ecosystem that has been undercovered in the existing literature. title: IU’s Luddy School digitizes Revolutionary War artifacts
content: "The 3-D digitization will take pictures all around the object and process them, using a photogrammetric procedure which identifies common features in the different images. The process orients the images in space and then performs what’s called the calibration of the camera, Guidi said. Once these steps are completed, image matching will automatically generate a dense cloud of 3-D points. This leads to generating the mesh, which is the model, the shape of the object, and its texture, he said. “You have to take several photographs around the object, and then you merge them and you process them in such a way…(that) gives you a digital twin of the physical object,” he said. “A digital twin means that also the size is totally the same, so it can be measured and analyzed, and this is very useful if you want to study something.” Possible challenges will be digitizing shiny or transparent objects because they are not compatible with the optical process used to generate the model. Guidi said they have dealt with this issue before in past projects and should be able to solve it this time. content: "This blog post argues that the next stage of AI evolution should move beyond isolated open initiatives toward Open AI Infrastructure: a systems architecture that integrates open models, open compute, open networking, and open orchestration into an interoperable execution fabric. Rather than proposing another initiative, Open AI Infrastructure provides the architectural framework that enables existing initiatives to operate together as a distributed intelligent system."

title: Altmetrics and Traditional Citation Impact among Top Iranian Researchers: A Comparative Analysis of ResearchGate and Academia
content: Abstract: Objective: The rapid expansion of digital communication has introduced alternative indicators of research visibility and impact, transforming traditional scholarly evaluation. This study investigates the potential of academic social networks for assessing the scholarly impact of Iranian researchers through an altmetrics approach. Method: This study employed a quantitative, cross-sectional design focused on the top 1% of Iranian researchers, as identified by the Islamic World Science Citation Center (ISC). Using a stratified sampling method, a sample of 203 researchers was selected across diverse disciplines. Data were collected between June 22, 2025, and June 4, 2026, by retrieving article-level metrics from Scopus, ResearchGate, and Academia.edu. Spearman’s rank correlation coefficient was applied to examine the relationship between Scopus citation counts and platform-specific engagement indicators (reads and views). Results: The analysis revealed a statistically significant positive correlation between Scopus citations and ResearchGate reads (r = 0.525). title: Power, Equity, and the Future of Open - SPARC
content: "Building on our popular “Open Access 101” events, SPARC is pleased to announce a new series, Collections & Open Access: Resourcing Open Scholarship, that will dive deeper into topics at the intersection of library collections and Open Access. This series will examine how collections librarians are navigating major changes, including funder public access requirements and evolving publisher business models, and consider what these changes mean for the future of libraries. The series will explore broader trends in the evolution of collections work, the practical realities of how different libraries are approaching these changes, and what lessons other institutions might draw from their experience. Resourcing Open Access is a three-part webinar series designed for collections-focused librarians and others engaged in this work. Together, we will move from foundational concepts to implementation to critical reflection—exploring not only how this work gets done, but why it matters and for whom. title: Available: OA Switchboard plugin for OJS 3.5 | OA Switchboard
content:
Supporting Diamond journals in increasing the visibility of their open access output among research funders, institutions and consortia.

The integration plugin connecting Open Journal Systems (OJS) with the OA Switchboard is now compatible with OJS 3.5.0.x. Journals running OJS 3.5 can start using the plugin right away.

Once enabled, the plugin automatically sends a set of public article metadata to relevant research funders and institutions via the OA Switchboard when an article is published. The metadata is captured at the point of publication and shared with the institutions affiliated with the article’s authors and the funders supporting the underlying research.

This happens automatically, with no additional manual work required from the editorial team, helping diamond open access journals make their published research more visible to the organisations that fund and support it.

title: Don’t Build Another Repository: Building Research Data Support Without Duplicating Infrastructure
content: "When universities begin thinking seriously about open research data, one solution appears almost immediately: build a repository. It sounds logical. It sounds ambitious. It sounds like progress. But at Wrocław University of Science and Technology, the Library asked a different question: what do researchers need first – another platform or a clearer path? Our answer was not to build new infrastructure. It was to build support. The Library launched a dedicated Open Research Data Section around real moments of need: preparing DMPs, understanding FAIR practice, deciding where data should go, and getting help early enough to matter. Instead of launching a standalone repository, we created a curated institutional pathway through RepOD. This allowed us to invest where local impact was greatest: developing librarians into data steward roles, guiding researchers through decisions, and cooperating with the University Project Department so that support begins at proposal stage, not at the end. This poster tells a simple story: transformation does not always begin with building something new. Sometimes it begins by choosing connection over duplication. title: Diamond Open Access publishing practices among researchers in Ghana | PLOS One
content: Abstract: The rise of Diamond Open Access (DOA) represents a major transformation in scholarly communication, redefining traditional systems of knowledge distribution. Diamond open access model has gained recognition as the most equitable and sustainable form of open access publishing. This study aimed to assess the awareness, perception and knowledge of DOA publishing practices among researchers in Ghana. A cross-sectional study design was used to conveniently collect data from 237 researchers across various institutions in Ghana. Data were collected using structured questionnaires Via Microsoft Forms and analysed using STATA version 17. Descriptive statistics, t-tests, ANOVA, factor analysis, Fisher’s exact test and logistic regression were conducted to identify patterns and relationships in the data. Statistical significance was set at p < 0.05 with a 95% confidence interval. Over half of the participants had no prior experience with Open Access (OA) publishing whilst about two-third of them had never heard of DOA. title: Public Access, Open Access, and the Need for NIH Governance | Health Policy | JAMA Internal Medicine | JAMA Network
content: Abstract:  In July 2025, the National Institutes of Health (NIH) Public Access Policy took effect, marking a landmark commitment to free immediate access to taxpayer-funded research. The policy requires that author accepted manuscripts from NIH-funded research be made publicly available in PubMed Central (PMC) immediately on publication, replacing an earlier policy that allowed publishers a 12-month embargo between publication and free public access.1 Several of the largest publishers have responded by requiring NIH-funded authors to pay open access article processing charges (APCs) to deposit the article in PMC. Although the NIH has stated that compliance does not require APC payment,2 it has not publicly defended this position against publisher practices to the contrary. This Viewpoint examines the resulting confusion between public access and open access, the pay-to-comply publisher practices that conflate the two, and the steps that the NIH must take to fill this gap and promote its public access goals.

title: Stop paying predatory publishers of academic journals—A policy proposal to restore scientific integrity and transparency - Rainey - FEBS Letters - Wiley Online Library
content: Abstract:  Scientific publishing is undergoing a systemic breakdown. Thousands of journals now collect article processing charges (APCs)—increasingly paid from public research funds—while providing minimal editorial oversight. This erodes standards, distorts incentives and threatens public trust in science. APC payments to six major publishers exceeded 8 billion dollars between 2019 and 2023, with almost no transparency over how these fees are set or spent. This cannot continue. We propose that public and institutional funds support journals—whether through APCs, subscriptions or bundled agreements—only where they are accredited against a transparent, enforceable quality standard. Implemented in stages and led by funding bodies and learned societies, such accreditation would narrow the space in which predatory journals operate without resorting to blacklists.

title: Public Access to NIH-Funded Research Manuscripts—Ensuring Dissemination Without Shifting Costs to Scientists | Health Policy | JAMA Internal Medicine | JAMA Network
content: Abstract:  The National Institutes of Health (NIH) has a strong interest in ensuring that the knowledge arising from research it funds is available to the scientific community and the general public. A key contributor to the Open Science movement, the NIH has embraced a variety of strategies, including clinical trial registration,1 data sharing, results reporting, and, most recently, immediate public access to manuscripts that arise from NIH funding. In aggregate, these efforts represent a 2-decade arc from encouragements to mandates toward ensuring that scientific knowledge is accessible to those who funded it—the US taxpayer.

title: Leveraging knowledge management to enhance research access and visibility via institutional repositories in South African universities | Digital Library Perspectives | Emerald Publishing
content: Abstract: Purpose This study aims to examine how South African universities are applying knowledge management practices to enhance the effectiveness of institutional repositories in improving research access and visibility. Design/methodology/approach The research was conducted using a qualitative content analysis, gathering data from secondary sources and organising it according to the stages of knowledge management: knowledge capture, organisation and storage, dissemination and application. Findings All universities in South Africa have implemented repositories, yet their alignment with knowledge management outcomes is lacking. Poor alignment between repository goals and knowledge management outcomes, limited institutional support, fragmentation and siloed practices contributed to the underutilisation of repository systems.
